anti_generic_signature_read: 'Some of it is memorable. The terrain tiles are the strongest idea: real sunken squares with modelled relief -- a dished crater rimmed with tiny pyramids, standing cones on the ice and desert tiles -- so the board has actual topography rather than printed art. The single all-black tile amid the turquoise is a striking, legible "danger square". The pairing of a dedicated 8-well tray per player with an 8-body planet set is a tidy, specific piece of design.' Against it, and recorded as given: 'the pieces themselves are close to a stock version of "planets as game tokens": sphere-on-chip, with textures at the level of a children's classroom poster.'
blind_action_read: 'Two players sit on opposite sides and move the ball-topped pieces from cell to cell across the grid, presumably with the terrain tiles modifying or blocking movement, and park captured or unplayed pieces in the scooped trays at the side. Physically, you would pick a piece up by the sphere or pinch the base, lift and set it down in a recessed cell.'
blind_form_read: 'The board is a thin slab, roughly twice as long as it is wide, with a raised outer lip and a grid of square recessed cells... a lattice of low grey ridges, with each cell sunk a few millimetres below the ridge tops.' Terrain read as dropped into the recesses: 'brown tiles carrying a large round crater dish surrounded by a fringe of little pyramids, turquoise tiles engraved with a radiating sunburst line pattern, orange tiles with the same sunburst, one solid black tile, and one pale sand-coloured slab that sits *above* the surface rather than sunk into it.' Pieces: 'a squat cylindrical base (a disc roughly two to three times the diameter of its height, with a tiny glyph stamped on the rim) with a sphere resting on top. Sphere diameters vary a lot between pieces... Each sphere has a small circular flange or collar where it meets the base. Two ringed spheres carry a large flat annulus tilted around them. Bases come in exactly two colours, white and black.'
blind_held_read: Unprompted, before knowing what the object was: 'A tabletop board game set: one flat rectangular playing board with a recessed grid, a set of ball-topped playing pieces that stand on round bases, and two separate flat storage/staging trays with scooped wells to park the pieces in.' On one piece alone: 'a marble-sized planet glued to a poker-chip-shaped base.'
blind_relationship_read: 'Each sphere sits on its own base; each base sits in (or across) a grid cell. White-based pieces cluster on the near-left half of the board and black-based pieces on the far-right half in view-1, which reads as a deliberate two-player opposition. The trays sit off the board entirely... sixteen wells total, exactly matching the sixteen pieces (eight per colour), which looks deliberate and well judged. The terrain tiles form clusters rather than scatter: a block of brown crater tiles occupies the board's middle, a turquoise cluster sits in one corner region around the black tile, and an orange cluster sits in the opposite corner region -- an intentional-looking three-zone layout.'
blind_subjects_read: Enumerated unprompted: 'Planets, with fairly high confidence overall, since the set is exactly eight bodies per colour.' Named individually with self-rated confidence: Jupiter ('orange-tan with horizontal bands and a red oval spot', very confident), Saturn ('pale yellow banded ball with a wide flat ring', very confident), Earth ('blue with green continents and white polar/cloud patches', very confident), Mars (confident), an ice giant in cyan, Neptune in deeper blue, 'Venus or a similar rocky body -- cream/pale gold with one wavy white band', moderate confidence, and 'Mercury or a cratered moon'. Terrain: 'the brown crater tiles read as an asteroid field or cratered ground (confident)'. 'No text, numbers, logos or figures are legible anywhere; the base rim glyphs are sub-pixel blobs.'

critical_form_requirements.blind_evidence: Cold, with no idea which piece mattered, the critic listed this world's colour regions as '(1) the large pale-gold body' and in the fresh look called it 'a butter-yellow ball' and, on the dimmer face, 'a warm khaki-ochre'. Every unprompted description of it is in the yellow-gold family and none mentions pink or cream-pink; asked afterwards it confirmed 'there is no pink anywhere'.
critical_form_requirements.requirement: Venus's globe is a saturated golden amber, not the pale pink-cream `beige` it carried before.

critical_form_requirements.blind_evidence: Blind, enumerating the sphere's colour regions before knowing what they were: '(2) a single silver-white band... (3) a small dark brown angular patch at the lower left of the ball', plus the globe body and the seat flange. Two marking tones, one above the globe and one below it, counted without being told to look for two.
critical_form_requirements.requirement: Venus carries exactly two marking tones beyond the globe, one brighter and one darker.

critical_form_requirements.blind_evidence: Blind: 'a single silver-white band, about a tenth of the ball's height, running horizontally across the lower-middle and dipping in a shallow V near the centre, with a wavy upper and lower edge'. One band, edge to edge, with non-parallel wavy edges -- read as continuous and irregular before the critic knew any feature had a name.
critical_form_requirements.requirement: The brighter tone draws the highlands, and the largest of them reads as one long continuous sinuous highland rather than a chain of separate blobs.

critical_form_requirements.blind_evidence: Blind, the darker tone was seen as a distinct region of its own on two different faces. On re-judgement against the requirement as written the critic found the subtraction directly visible: 'the cocoa area's corner is cut off in a straight line exactly where the grey patch begins', and measuring every lowland boundary pixel in three frames, 'in no frame is there a single pixel of cocoa lying over grey'.
critical_form_requirements.requirement: The darker tone draws the lowland plains from the three supplied plains rings, with the highlands subtracted out of them so the highland wins where the two overlap.

critical_form_requirements.blind_evidence: Blind the critic reported 'scattered hexagonal patches' and counted their sides; primed, it measured them as 'a closed polygon with six straight sides and six sharp corners... None is a circle: a circle has no corners and these have six, resolved cleanly. None is a dot', at 7% to 15% of the globe's diameter. That is exactly what a six-vertex supplied ring drawn unmoved produces.
critical_form_requirements.requirement: The markings are drawn as outlines from the supplied rings -- no marking is a circle and none was shrunk to a dot.

critical_form_requirements.blind_evidence: The blind read was demonstrably alert to relief -- it reported the belt tiles' 'fringe of little pyramids' and standing cones elsewhere in the same images -- and reported no raised or sunken edge anywhere on this globe. Measured afterwards on the overhead frame: 'radius mean 197.4 px, min 196.2, max 198.4, std 0.28% -- a true circle with no bump anywhere on the limb', with 'no thickness, no edge shadow and no shading discontinuity' at the patch boundaries.
critical_form_requirements.requirement: Every marking on Venus is a flush colour inlay: the globe's outer surface is still a true sphere, nothing protrudes and no downward-facing surface was added.

critical_form_requirements.blind_evidence: Blind: 'the identical sphere, identical band shape, identical brown patch and identical camera angle, but the base is black and the rim glyph is white. This is the same item as view-3 with only the base colour swapped'. The same map on both, the ownership cue inverted. The critic also recorded, correctly, that the lean itself is not a visible cue on this world -- at 177.36 degrees of obliquity the two armies' leans differ by 5.28 degrees, and it measured the fitted belt tilt differing by 2.4 degrees between them.
critical_form_requirements.requirement: The two Venus pieces are mirrors of one another: the same map, with the ownership cue inverted.

critical_form_requirements.blind_evidence: Blind, with no prompt about any risk of confusion, the critic listed them as two separate planets and rated Saturn 'very confident': 'Saturn -- pale yellow banded ball with a wide flat ring'. Shown them side by side afterwards: 'Saturn is obviously the bigger piece, boldly striped in orange-brown and wrapped in a broad white ring tilted steeply'. It never confused them at any point.
critical_form_requirements.requirement: Venus and Saturn are still told apart now that both globes are yellow-amber.

critical_form_requirements.blind_evidence: Blind, the critic enumerated this sphere's colour regions exhaustively and orange is not among them: pale gold body, silver-white band, dark brown patch, white sliver, gold flange. It named orange readily elsewhere in the same images -- Jupiter, the corona tiles, the flames -- so it was not blind to the colour. Confirmed on the pixels afterwards: 'Zero pixels anywhere on the globe in any of the four frames'.
critical_form_requirements.requirement: NEGATIVE: there is no orange anywhere on Venus.

critical_form_requirements.blind_evidence: Blind, the sphere was read as 'cream/pale gold with one wavy white band' and its regions counted as five; no Y, no swirl and no cloud appears anywhere in the unprompted description. Checked afterwards: 'no circular marking of any kind survives -- I found no circles at all, so the old ten-circle cloud Y is fully gone, not merely faded'.
critical_form_requirements.requirement: NEGATIVE: there is no cloud pattern on Venus -- no Y, no swirl, no atmospheric banding.

critical_form_requirements.blind_evidence: The blind read reported deliberate grit where it exists in this set -- the belt tile's 'ring of discrete flat-topped boulders' -- and reported none on this globe. Confirmed afterwards: 'All three materials render as flat, uninterrupted areas.'
critical_form_requirements.requirement: NEGATIVE: no stippling, grit, speckle or fine ribbing stands in for the reference's texture.

critical_form_requirements.blind_evidence: Blind, the critic looked straight down what it took to be the piece's axis and found no planet there at all: of view-8 it wrote 'plainly: nothing but a base... No sphere, no colour, no detail.' That frame is the camera aimed down Venus's true north pole, and an unprimed reader finding the disc's underside there is exactly the evidence that this world's north pole points into the board. The pole region that is visible is the south one, in `venus-<side>-south-polar.png`.
critical_form_requirements.requirement: NEGATIVE: the 177.36 degree obliquity was not corrected -- Venus's map still reads inverted.

largest_risk: The highland filament, and it is the reviewer's finding rather than this build's. Asked directly whether Venus reads as the same planet as the Magellan reference, the critic answered no on the Aphrodite face and 'arguable' on the other, and named the reason precisely: on the reference the bright highland terrain is warmer and yellower than the ground it sits on -- it measured hue 38 at saturation 0.66 against a ground of hue 30 at 0.83 -- whereas `beige` #F7E6DE is hue 19.2 at saturation 0.10 against a globe of #FFB549 at hue 35.6, so the piece's bright tone is pinker and cooler than its globe where the reference's is yellower and warmer. The hue relationship is inverted. It recorded this as a disagreement with the Wish, which names that filament. Two things bound it. The images overstate it: the review renderer encodes sRGB twice, taking the highland from saturation 0.10 to 0.04 and the globe from 0.71 to 0.43, so the plastic is warmer than any image here shows, and the critic withdrew its own phrase 'neutral grey' as a description of the part. And the palette cannot fix it: `measure/venus-highland-palette.md` checks all nineteen stocked filaments against the three conditions -- brighter than the globe, in the reference's warm hue band, carrying real chroma -- and only `yellow` #FFD834 passes, which separates 9.6 luma levels from the globe in the canonical render against `beige`'s 20.2, the weakest marking separation in the set, and which is Saturn's own globe filament. The finding is real, it is recorded in the product's limitations in the critic's own terms, and it is not repairable with the plastics this shop stocks.
resolution:
PROTOCOL. The critic got eight canonical images copied into a scratch directory as view-1 ... view-8 so no file path could prime it, no Wish, no concept, no product name, and a rule that reading any other file voided the review. Its blind read was fixed before anything was revealed. Round two was primed and said so: told it already knew the Wish, told nothing in that round could count as naive recognition, and asked for fresh observations of three images before comparing anything to a requirement. No geometry changed between rounds.

OUTCOME. Round one gave a real unprimed read -- it named the object as a two-player planet board game and read the size ladder, the two armies, the terrain zones and the tray-to-piece count unprompted -- plus three blocking defects. Two were verdicts against my paraphrase, not the Wish: I had written 'broad' plains and outlines 'with irregular edges', neither of which the Wish says. Given the exact wording it re-judged both as met, having measured the subtraction first: 'in no frame is there a single pixel of cocoa lying over grey.' The third, that the plains are sparse on the Aphrodite face, came with a suggested fix -- re-aim the camera. I tested it instead of arguing: across 360 degrees of azimuth, Aphrodite peaks at 1.00 with the plains at 0.44, and the plains peak at 2.00 with Aphrodite at 0.21, because Venus's plains lie away from Aphrodite. No camera shows both. measure/venus-facing.md is that sweep; the critic accepted it and withdrew the blocker.

It also withdrew two of its own blind findings after looking harder -- Saturn's ring as an interpenetration, and two adjacent pieces as interpenetrating discs. Its seven non-blocking observations are carried into product.json in its own words, including the filament objection, recorded as a disagreement with the Wish rather than resolved away. That nothing outside Venus changed is settled by measure/occurrence-geometry.md, not by images: 162 labels identical, changed-geometry 'None'.
reviewer: One independent native critic, given the canonical images under neutral filenames and no Wish, concept or product name; its unprimed read was recorded and fixed before anything was revealed.
